圖像加註文字，特朗普、習近平、普京在11月18日深圳舉行的APEC峰會晚宴上。
你可能有過這樣的經歷：你和兩位朋友平時都經常聯繫，他們彼此也見過面，但三個人湊齊坐在同一張飯桌上的機會卻屈指可數。
習近平、特朗普（Donald Trump）和普京（Vladimir Putin），就處在有些相似的微妙狀態裡。
他們上一次同框還是七年前，而三人更從未舉行過正式的三方會談。不過，正在深圳召開的亞太經合組織（APEC）峰會為中美俄領導人坐在一起創造了罕見機會。這場安排在峰會最後一天舉行的場邊會晤，受到的關注甚至超過了峰會本身。
從核武器，到人工智能，從烏克蘭，到伊朗戰事，一系列全球熱點議題都可能出現在三人的討論議程上。儘管有美國官員暗示，此次會晤不會討論烏克蘭戰爭。
「他們能坐下來，就說明這個世界還沒有到第一次或第二次世界大戰那個狀況。」香港科技大學榮休教授丁學良對BBC說。
但這場會晤也引發了一些擔憂。烏克蘭總統澤連斯基（Volodymyr Zelensky）上個月公開表示：「我們絕不希望看到局面演變成某種『雅爾塔2.0、3.0或4.0』，導致勢力範圍的重新劃分。」日本和韓國的外交官據報也表達了擔憂。
那麼，在全球貿易保護主義升溫、地緣政治競爭加劇之際，深圳究竟會見證一場凝聚亞太共識的多邊峰會，還是淪為三個大國重新劃定權力邊界的博弈場？
圖像加註文字，習近平罕見地親自前往機場迎接特朗普。
週三，深圳機場的停機坪上，普京的伊爾-96和特朗普的「空軍一號」在凌晨和下午先後到達。儘管這個中國南方科技之都早已進入嚴密安保狀態，多條道路被封鎖，仍有大量市民在車隊經過的道路旁圍觀等候。
今年5月，特朗普與普京已經前後腳訪問了北京。但在許多觀察者看來，能夠出席APEC峰會並舉行中美俄三方會談，對莫斯科而言，仍具有突破外交孤立的象徵意義。這從克里姆林宮今年10月率先放風「美中俄峰會」可見一斑。
自2022年俄羅斯全面入侵烏克蘭以來，莫斯科與西方國家的關係持續惡化，普京被國際刑事法院簽發逮捕令，這使其缺席了多項原本由他親自出席的大型多邊會議。外訪也主要集中在亞洲的戰略夥伴國家。
「普京是三位領導人中最有可能從這次會談中獲益的人。」亞洲協會政策研究所（Asia Society Policy Institute）中國分析中心研究員高世明（Aaron Glasserman）對BBC說。他稱，普京需要向國內展示，俄羅斯仍然是一個與美國和中國平起平坐的大國。
圖像加註文字，普京週三凌晨抵達深圳機場。中方派出中共中央政治局常委蔡奇迎接。
對克里姆林宮而言，會談的政治畫面本身就可能是一種成果。高世明認為，如果會議的影像或聲明讓外界認為華盛頓已接受俄羅斯對部分烏克蘭領土的主權主張，或不再支持烏克蘭的抵抗，對莫斯科而言都將是重大外交勝利。
但華盛頓的目光顯然落在別處。白宮在峰會前指出，特朗普將與習近平和普京討論「削減全球核武器」的議題，並認為核武器擴散極其危險。
美國與俄羅斯之間最後一項具有法律約束力的主要戰略核武器限制條約——《新削減戰略武器條約》（New START）——已於2026年2月5日到期。這意味著，兩國自半個多世紀以來，首次不再受到具有法律約束力的戰略核武器數量限制。
特朗普早在第一任期內便提出，希望建立一套新的核軍控安排，並將中國納入談判，因為中國的核武庫正在進行快速擴張。但北京持續拒絕這一提議，認為美俄應先大幅削減自身核武庫，再談其他核武國家的參與。
高世明表示，特朗普希望借由與兩位大國領導人直接接觸，塑造自己能夠推動和平、維持全球穩定的形象。而在共和黨中期選舉慘敗、失去參眾兩院控制權後，一場具有象徵意義的外交勝利，有助於他向國內展示外交成果。
「畢竟，阻止德黑蘭獲得核武器，已成為美國進行那場代價高昂且不得人心的伊朗戰爭的主要藉口。」他補充道。
多名受訪專家認為，北京不可能在核武器問題上輕易讓步。丁學良表示，這在奉行實用主義的中國看來是一種「白日夢」。而中國全球化智庫（CCG）副主任高志凱則說，特朗普的核談判是美國和前蘇聯談判的延續，對中國來說是「把蘋果和橘子拿來作比較」（compare apples to oranges）。
而有分析認為，習近平能從此次會晤中獲得的利益最少。這也是中國遲遲到本週一才確認將舉行三方會晤的原因。外交部發言人此前持續表示，北京「同有關方保持著溝通」。
「習近平致力於展示中國已躋身全球權力中心，但與普京相比，他從此次會晤中獲益有限，畢竟今年他已參與了多場高規格峰會。」高世明說。
在香蜜湖旁，APEC峰會主場館深圳國際交流中心如同一隻展翅的大鵬。它的背後是高樓林立的福田金融和商務核心區。這座城市是中國經濟騰飛的起點，也被視為是中國改革開放最成功的象徵。
當局顯然希望透過深圳展現其國家實力——不僅在於過去和現在，還在於未來。一批從深圳崛起的科技企業，如今已在全球產業與技術競爭中扮演關鍵角色。
這或許也解釋了為何中美俄領導人會晤引發了截然不同的解讀。有人從中看到穩定的希望，但包括澤連斯基在內的人擔心，這將成為另一次雅爾塔時刻。
1945年，美、蘇、英三國領導人在克里米亞城市雅爾塔劃分了勢力範圍，為戰後國際秩序奠定了基礎。但這場會議也成為大國繞過小國、私下決定其命運的象徵。
在當時，中國正是「被決定命運」的一方。為換取蘇聯對日作戰，美國和英國同意給予莫斯科在中國的特殊權益。然而，作為反法西斯戰爭的盟友，中國卻被排除在這些談判之外，對相關安排毫不知情。
圖像加註文字，雅爾塔會議成為大國繞過小國、私下決定其命運的象徵。
「當年雅爾塔做的決定是傷害了中國的國家利益的。」高志凱對BBC說。「所以中國絕不會走這條老路。」
分析師們認為，更重要的是，三個大國雖然可能坐在同一張桌子前，卻並不意味著它們對世界秩序有共同的構想。「他們的利益訴求各不相同，有時甚至存在衝突。」高世明說。
「習近平需要在國內展現大國地位與國際上反對霸權主義之間尋求平衡。如果中國被視為與美俄一道瓜分勢力範圍，或是插手他國內政，這在國際觀感上將非常不利。」高世明說。
他指出，烏克蘭問題尤其如此。北京希望避免進一步疏遠歐洲各國政府，因為中國仍在與歐盟就貿易和投資問題持續談判。
這或許能解釋北京為何在烏克蘭問題上顯得跋前躓後。德國總統施泰因邁爾（Frank-Walter Steinmeier）在上個月訪問北京後稱，當他向習近平詢問中美俄峰會將討論結束烏克蘭戰爭的問題時，習近平「似乎有些困惑」。
「你可以看出他臉上的不悅。他甚至問，這些傳言是從哪裡來的。」施泰因邁爾說。「他明確表示，這是一場歐洲的衝突，歐洲人自己必須參與解決。」
「因為北京知道，對世界擁有更多影響力的同時，是要付出代價的。」丁學良說。他表示，儘管中國希望成為「大國」和「強國」，但「算盤一直打得很清楚」。
他以伊朗衝突舉例說，儘管中國是伊朗石油的重要買家，美國、以色列和伊朗的戰爭導致中國利益受損嚴重，但北京「絕不會因此選擇直接介入軍事衝突」。
儘管如此，許多國際頭條在報道這次峰會時，仍常用「歷史首次」來形容美、中、俄三個核大國最高領導人的握手。
萊頓大學（Leiden University）資深講師王珏（Jue Wang；音譯）博士認為，鑑於三國在核安全、國際衝突和全球戰略穩定方面的影響力，此次三方會談具有重要的地緣政治象徵意義。但她表示，其實際影響仍取決於能否產生具體協議。
「在這三個國家之間達成協議並非此次會議的目標之一。」她對BBC說。「因為此次三方會晤是在APEC間隙舉行，而它並不是一個用於磋商重大地緣政治或安全協議的機制。」
還有人認為，特朗普在中期選舉遭遇重創後，其許多外交決策都將面臨國會更嚴格的審視，這使其能實際發揮的空間變得有限，尤其是對俄政策上。
「如果特朗普向俄羅斯做出進一步讓步，必將面臨國內巨大的政治阻力。」高世明說。
儘管此次會晤不太可能有實質性成果，但王珏相信，美中兩國在戰略競爭的同時，仍擁有重要的「共同利益」，包括AI安全、清潔能源、流行病防控、國際貿易與供應鏈韌性，以及打擊跨國犯罪等。
「在這些領域，兩國無需放棄技術競爭，也無需解決根本性的政治分歧，即可展開合作。」她補充說。
即使這場會晤最終沒有達成實質性協議，從基輔到東京和首爾的反應已足夠表明，在地緣競爭日益激烈的今天，許多中小經濟體正擔心自己的聲音變得越來越微弱。
新加坡國立大學政治系副教授莊嘉穎表示，如果世界變成由不同大國主宰不同的區域，這會縮小中小國家的自主空間。而它們面臨的另一個困境，是國際法和國際組織近年來「持續被強權國家所掏空」。
他舉例說，美國在特朗普的領導下，退出了氣候公約、大幅削減對聯合國機構的資助，這帶來直接的衝擊。而中國則在間接上進行弱化，比如無視南海仲裁案的裁決，持續在南海填海造島。俄羅斯更是直接入侵烏克蘭。
「二戰之後長期建立起來的這套體系，原本是對大國有一定約束力，並在一定程度上讓中小國家至少在法理上和大國可以平起平坐。而當這個體系被弱化，中小國家的議價能力會被明顯削弱。」莊嘉穎對BBC說。
加拿大總理卡尼（Mark Carney）便是其中之一。今年1月，他在達沃斯論壇發表演講時，呼籲中等強國聯合起來，因為「如果不在餐桌上，就會在菜單上」。
這一理念也得到了堪培拉的支持。外交部長黃英賢也在一場演講中稱，中等強國正在努力促成平衡格局，「確保沒有任何國家一家獨大」。
圖像加註文字，北京希望藉此次APEC展現其經濟和科技實力。
不過，中小國家並非只能被動應對大國競爭。儘管它們在軍事和政治影響力上難以與大國抗衡，但在全球經濟體系中，大國同樣無法忽視它們的作用。無論是商品市場、關鍵礦產，還是區域供應鏈和貿易網絡，中小經濟體都佔據著重要位置。
約翰斯·霍普金斯大學（Johns Hopkins University）講席教授洪源遠（Yuen Yuen Ang）專注於中國和新興市場的政治經濟和發展研究。她對BBC表示，對北京而言，區域貿易關係的重要性只增不減。
「中國領導人認識到，全球化的黃金時代已經結束，貿易保護主義和地緣經濟競爭已成為新常態。」她說道，由於中國仍高度依賴海外市場，北京有更強烈的動機推動區域貿易合作。
高世明也有類似的看法。他認為，儘管中美俄領導人會面可能在此次APEC峰會上顯得喧賓奪主，但對中國而言，與貿易夥伴的關係相當重要。
「全球範圍內對全球化所帶來的經濟和社會後果的反對聲浪日益高漲。然而，中國對海外市場的依賴程度卻達到了前所未有的高度。」他說道。
中國與東南亞國家之間的貿易，反映了這種經濟聯繫的深度。2020年，東盟超越美國，成為中國最大的貿易夥伴。中國商品在東盟進口市場中的佔比，從2005年的10.6%上升至2024年的25.5%。
與此同時，東盟秘書處與聯合國2025年發佈的一份報告顯示，2020至2023年，東盟有超過75%的關鍵礦產出口流向中國。
「現在發生在深圳的這一切最大的意義是，全球仍脫離不了國際合作。」丁學良說。「現在並不是八十年前。」

content:
2026年11月18日，各國領導人在深圳舉行的亞太經合組織（APEC）峰會的歡迎晚宴前準備合影。(Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images)
【大紀元2026年11月19日訊】（大紀元記者趙彬、易如採訪報導）深圳APEC峰會期間，各國領袖受到的接待規格差異明顯。習近平親自迎接美國總統特朗普，俄羅斯總統普京由中共政治局常委蔡奇接機，韓國總統李在明等人獲安排迎賓隊伍，日本首相高市早苗卻只獲低調接待。
專家指出，中共將雙邊政治分歧帶入多邊峰會，把東道主的公共職責變成政治工具，涉嫌「公器私用」。
11月18日，各國領袖陸續抵達深圳出席APEC峰會。特朗普獲得最高規格接待，習近平親自到深圳寶安機場迎接，現場安排軍方儀仗隊、手持中美兩國國旗和鮮花的歡迎隊伍，還有戰機飛越致敬。兩人下機後握手並短暫擁抱。
普京抵達時，由中共政治局常委蔡奇到機場迎接，現場同樣安排青年迎賓隊伍。韓國總統李在明夫婦抵達時，則由廣東省政協主席林克慶等官員迎接，現場也有青年迎賓隊伍。加拿大總理卡尼、馬來西亞首相安華等領袖抵達時，也有迎賓隊伍及相應安排。
高市早苗的待遇則明顯不同。中方安排已退休的前駐希臘大使章啟月，以外交部禮賓大使身分接機。現場雖有儀仗隊，但沒有部分國家領袖抵達時出現的青年迎賓隊伍、鮮花及歡呼場面。
接待差異還延伸到下機安全安排。日本媒體人矢板明夫根據電視畫面目測，高市所乘飛機的機艙出口與舷梯平台之間，落差約有40公分。畫面顯示，高市需要扶著機門，小心跨出第一步。中國網絡上有人以「不給台階下」嘲諷這一安排。
日本前防衛副大臣、外務副大臣中山泰秀在社群平台X轉發相關畫面，質疑機艙出口與舷梯之間為何有如此大的落差。他表示，高市穿著裙裝和高跟鞋，若下機時失足受傷，後果由誰負責，並要求中方說明舷梯設置及安全檢查情況。
晚宴入場時的音樂安排也引起議論。樂團按照不同領袖所屬國家演奏歌曲，特朗普入場時演奏《美麗的美利堅》，普京入場時演奏《俄羅斯舞曲》，高市入場時則演奏日本歌手坂本九的名曲《上を向いて歩こう》，中文常譯為《昂首向前走》，英文歌名為《Sukiyaki》。
這首1961年推出的歌曲，歌詞描寫一個人獨自抬頭走路，不讓眼淚落下。有輿論認為，選用這首日本名曲只是為了營造歡迎氣氛；也有網民將歌詞中「獨自一人強忍淚水」的意象，解讀為暗示高市處於孤立境地。
對於高市受到的接待規格，日本內閣官房長官木原稔11月19日在記者會上表示，高市接受的是APEC「輪值國的標準待遇」。對於高市在機場受到的歡迎儀式比其他國家領袖「簡單」的差異，木原表示，日方「無權評論其它國家的禮儀安排」。
中國民主黨全國委員會共同主席王軍濤接受大紀元採訪時指出，在國際性多邊峰會上按照雙邊關係安排不同接待規格，是將公共職責用於傳遞政治訊息，屬於「公器私用」。
他解釋，兩國關係不好時，在只涉及雙邊關係的場合，通過接待規格高低向對方釋放外交信號，是可以理解的操作。但APEC並不是中日兩國的交往場合。
「APEC峰會不是中日兩國的交往問題，是中國受所有成員國的委託，作為東道主舉辦這場國際會議，其職責是讓所有與會國都感到舒適、方便。」王軍濤說。
他指出，中共將雙邊外交矛盾帶入多邊會議，利用東道主身分向特定國家傳遞政治訊息，已經偏離了舉辦國際會議的公共職責。
王軍濤表示，這種做法不只會影響被冷落國家的觀感，也會讓其他參與者質疑中共能否公平對待不同國家，以及舉辦國際會議的誠意。外界也可能因此擔心，假如中共日後國力增強，是否會利用自身地位，在國際場合對待與其立場不合的國家。
他還批評習近平「不太守外交規定，也不太懂，所以失策了」。
台灣國防安全研究院研究員沈明室對大紀元表示，中共冷遇高市有兩個目的：一是藉接待安排向日本施壓，並向其它國家傳遞不服從中共立場就會受到冷遇的訊號；二是配合中共內部的政治需要。
沈明室指出，高市2025年11月表達「台灣有事」的立場，一年後仍表示不會收回相關發言，令中共惱怒。因此，習近平採取降低接待規格、不與高市會面等方式報復，刻意向她施壓。他認為，這是中共慣用的伎倆。
沈明室還分析，高市可能已在峰會前與特朗普會談時，談及在APEC期間可能遇到的問題，並確認美日同盟關係。
對於中共為何要在多邊峰會上展示強硬姿態，王軍濤提出另一層解釋。他認為，習近平的考量不完全是外交層面，而是要向國內展示強硬姿態。
「獨裁者做事更多不是從外交上考慮，而是要演給國內的人看。」王軍濤說，他認為習近平此舉也有鼓動國內民粹主義和反日情緒、藉此打壓日本的盤算。
王軍濤以1999年江澤民處理美中關係的一段往事為例。當時中共駐南斯拉夫使館遭轟炸，時任美國總統克林頓曾撥打美中熱線電話，王軍濤認為江澤民故意不接電話，是要向國內展示強硬姿態。
「這個不接，就是要演給中國人看：美國現在求我，我偏不給他這個面子。」王軍濤說，獨裁者需要民粹主義支撐。
對於這種做法的外交代價，沈明室認為，中共將外交禮遇政治化，必然引發日本輿論反彈，也讓其它國家看清北京的手段。中共即使展示強硬，也未必能使周邊國家聽從其立場，因為各國在關鍵時刻仍會觀察美國的態度。
王軍濤也認為，針對日本首相的接待安排，並不能讓中共在外交上取得實際利益，反而可能使其它APEC成員國感到寒心。他指出，這類做法會讓國際社會看到中共利用公共場合處理雙邊恩怨，也會損害習近平試圖與美國共同扮演國際領袖的形象。
習近平親自到機場迎接特朗普，與其它領袖的接機安排形成對比。中方將此解釋為對今年9月習近平訪美時，特朗普夫婦專程到機場迎接習近平的「禮尚往來」。
澳洲廣播公司（ABC）引述布魯金斯學會約翰‧桑頓中國中心主任瑞安‧哈斯（Ryan Hass）分析，北京最重要的目標，是盡可能延長中美關係「脆弱的平靜期」，因此習近平會在特朗普訪問期間尋找機會表達禮遇和尊重，親自到停機坪迎接便是其中一個例子。
王軍濤認為，特朗普此前高規格接待習近平，確實存在禮尚往來的因素，但外交互動從來都是政治博弈。他指出，美方此前在中共在意的台灣問題及高科技管制等方面並沒有作出實質讓步，而特朗普希望在貿易方面取得的成果，則仍在推進中。
王軍濤表示，接下來的中美會談，將能檢驗「禮尚往來」背後的政治博弈結果。
峰會期間，普京與習近平的一次握手互動也受到關注。從現場畫面看，普京走向習近平與特朗普所在位置時，先與特朗普握手。外界因此出現兩種解讀：一種認為普京有意跳過習近平，直接向特朗普示好；另一種則認為，普京原本是要與習近平握手，但習近平沒有及時回應，普京才轉而與特朗普握手。單憑畫面，目前難以確認當時的實際情況。
對於習近平為何沒有及時回應，王軍濤分析，習近平在國際外交場合的臨場反應不如朱鎔基、溫家寶等前任領導人。他認為，習近平的外交反應較為拘謹，習慣按照預定流程行事，普京當時的動作可能不在中方事先安排之內，令習近平一時不知如何應對。
沈明室則從中美俄關係分析，普京可能對中共的態度有所不滿。他指出，俄羅斯希望中共站在自己一邊，提供更多支持，甚至像北韓一樣明確支持俄羅斯，或增加購買俄羅斯能源等；但中共目前希望緩和與美國的關係，不敢因此得罪美國，因此不願公開大幅支持俄羅斯。
沈明室表示，中共對俄烏戰爭的立場有所保留，也不想得罪烏克蘭。在美國限制中國購買俄羅斯能源的情況下，北京更難公開擴大對俄支持。他認為，這正是當前中美俄關係中的矛盾：中共希望與美國改善關係，卻可能因此令俄羅斯感到不滿。

华盛顿——美国海军已选择帕特里克·芬尼少将担任新职务，重点推进海军核海上发射巡航导弹（[SLCM-N](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/slcm-n/)）和高超音速常规快速打击（[CPS](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/conventional-prompt-strike/)）武器系统在水面舰艇和潜艇上的集成。

芬尼是第一个领导位于印第安纳州海军武器站起重机的新项目管理办公室的人，并向投资组合采购执行战略系统项目总监道格拉斯·威廉姆斯中将报告。
印第安纳州共和党参议员吉姆·班克斯 (Jim Banks) 在周二的[参议院军事委员会](https://writingdefense.com/2026/11/lawmakers-challenge-trumps-push-to-bring-steam-catapults-back-to-ford-class/)听证会上公开确认芬尼是被选为该职位的军官，并指出芬尼已于 10 月份上任。海军没有正式宣布他被任命担任这一角色。

即便如此，班克斯在 5 月份首次宣布，国防部长皮特·赫格斯和[代理海军部长曹洪](https://breakdefense.com/2026/09/white-house-sends-caos-secnav-nomination-to-senate/) 决定在班克斯的家乡设立海军预备役一星上将的职位。克兰拥有高超音速研究、开发、测试和评估设施。

此后曹还提到了这个新角色，并表示该职位对于支持这两个武器计划至关重要——尽管五角大楼的范围更广

# Navy taps one-star admiral to advance hypersonic weapons, SLCM-N integration at Crane

Rear Adm. Patrick Finney is the first person to lead the new program management office based out of Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana.

By [Diana Stancy](https://breakingdefense.com/author/dstancy/) on November 18, 2026 3:41 pm

WASHINGTON — The Navy has selected Rear Adm. Patrick Finney for a new role focused on advancing the integration of the Navy’s Nuclear Sea Launch Cruise Missile ([SLCM-N](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/slcm-n/)) and hypersonic Conventional Prompt Strike ([CPS](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/conventional-prompt-strike/)) weapons systems onto surface vessels and submarines.

Finney is the first person to lead the new program management office based out of Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana, and reports to Vice Adm. Douglas Williams, the director of Portfolio Acquisition Executive Strategic Systems Programs.

Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., publicly identified Finney as the officer selected for the role Tuesday during a[Senate Armed Services Committee](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/11/lawmakers-challenge-trumps-push-to-bring-steam-catapults-back-to-ford-class/)hearing, noting Finney had arrived at his post in October. The Navy did not formally announce he’d been tapped for the role.

Even so, Banks first announced in May that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and [Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/09/white-house-sends-caos-secnav-nomination-to-senate/) had decided to create the position for a Navy Reserve one-star admiral in Banks’ home state. Crane is home to a hypersonics research, development, test and evaluation facility.

Cao has also mentioned the new role since then, saying the position was critical to supporting the two weapons programs— despite broader Pentagon efforts to cut down on the number of flag and general officers.

“We did this in a time when we’re reducing flag and general officers and looking for ways to streamline,” Cao said i n Octobe r at the Northeast Indiana Defense Summit. “But this is so important that we move the flag officer up here in order to focus on two critical weapon systems that will bring capability to our ships and aircraft.”

The Navy is currently modifying its Zumwalt-class destroyers with a vertical launch system to accommodate CPS missiles, and plans to equip some Virginia-class submarines with the system as well. The missile is being jointly developed with the Army, which is pursuing its own ground-launched version of the weapon under the Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon program, also known as Dark Eagle. Both services are seeking to pour more than $50 billion into the hypersonic effort, according to a [Government Accountability Report from July](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/07/navy-army-risk-wasting-money-time-without-unified-hypersonic-missile-strategy-gao/).

The program’s total acquisition cost is estimated at $15 billion to $20 billion, officials said in a separate [GAO report released in July](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/07/pentagon-continues-to-struggle-with-key-weapons-development-timelines-gao/). The Navy is targeting an initial operational capability by 2034, although program officials acknowledged that timeline is “aggressive,” per the GAO report.

Finney previously served on the Los Angeles-class submarines Atlanta and Dallas, as well as tours with Submarine Group 10 and Fleet Forces Command, [according to his official Navy biography](https://www.navy.mil/Leadership/Flag-Officer-Biographies/BioDisplay/Article/4614615/rear-admiral-patrick-finney/). 由于英伟达丑闻有可能在特朗普与习近平的会谈中重新引发贸易紧张局势，北京仍然持有稀土
随着第三十三次亚太经合组织（APEC）领导人会议本周在深圳开幕，中国制定了广泛的议程，包括推动亚太地区自由贸易路线图。虽然许多人都在关注中国国家主席习近平、美国总统唐纳德·特朗普和俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京本周四举行的最后一刻三边会议，但特朗普和习近平今年的第三次单独双边会谈将把经济问题带到人们的面前。上周爆发的英伟达丑闻加剧了紧张局势，而在华盛顿和北京都有理由维持 2025 年 10 月达成的休战协议之际，半导体出口管制也给贸易谈判带来了阴影。
美国先进半导体走私到中国，以及中国企业远程获取海外计算能力，长期以来一直令华盛顿担忧。 Nvidia-Megaspeed 争议中，一家新加坡云提供商因涉嫌将受限制的芯片转移到中国而受到调查，这进一步暴露了美国出口管制制度的潜在漏洞。 Megaspeed 否认有不当行为。这一事件引发了人们的疑问：出口管制是否能有效遏制中国的技术进步，以及美国如何堵住现有的漏洞。中美贸易往往一次形成一项经济限制和一项技术标准。从境外投资审查到各种实体清单和其他贸易限制，尽管贸易休战，双方都没有停止引入新的限制，而中国 2025 年 4 月的稀土出口许可要求仍然有效。
据报道，Megaspeed 前高管与英伟达 (Nvidia) 黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 有联系，针对其的中国间谍指控已经为国会和商务部提供了新的动力，以加强对半导体的控制。针对黄仁勋辞去英伟达首席执行官一职，中国问题特别委员会主席众议员约翰·穆勒纳尔（John Moolenaar）呼吁国会“迅速采取行动，在年底国防法案中通过两党出口管制立法”。目前的立法工作包括《人工智能监督法案》、《芯片安全法案》和《匹配法案》，其中提出了诸如芯片位置验证要求和半导体制造设备联合控制协调等措施。周末，商务部发布了一项临时最终规则，以解决远程访问计算能力的问题，尽管目前尚不清楚该规则将如何实施和执行。美国对先进芯片的更严格限制可能会招致北京方面通过加强稀土管制或恢复更广泛的限制来进行报复，中国最近将这些限制延长至 2027 年 1 月 10 日。
2025年4月，中国商务部、海关总署发布2025年第18号公告，对7种稀土元素实施出口管制。虽然没有明确针对美国，但中国在关键矿产供应链的主导地位在贸易战升级期间受到了严重影响。这些出口管制扰乱了供应链

As the Nvidia scandal threatens to reignite trade tensions at Trump-Xi talks, Beijing still holds the rare earths
As the thirty-third Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting begins this week in Shenzhen, China has set an expansive agenda, including pushing for a roadmap for Asia-Pacific-wide free trade. While many eyes are on the last-minute trilateral meeting among Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin this Thursday, the separate Trump and Xi bilateral, their third this year, will bring economic issues to the fore. The Nvidia scandal that broke last week has added to tensions, and semiconductor export controls loom over the trade negotiations at a moment when both Washington and Beijing have reason to preserve the truce struck in October 2025.
The smuggling of advanced US semiconductors into China, along with Chinese firms’ remote access to computing power abroad, have long concerned Washington. The Nvidia-Megaspeed controversy, in which a Singapore-based cloud provider is under investigation for allegedly diverting restricted chips to China, has further exposed potential gaps in the US export-control regime. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing. The incident has raised questions as to whether export controls are effective in containing Chinese technological advancement and how the US can close existing loopholes. US-China trade is often shaped one economic restriction and one technical standard at a time. From outbound investment screening to various entity lists and other trade restrictions, neither side has ceased introducing new restrictions despite the trade truce, and all the while China’s April 2025 rare earth export licensing requirements remain in force.
The Chinese espionage allegations surrounding a former Megaspeed executive with reported ties to Nvidia’s Jensen Huang have already given Congress and the Department of Commerce new fuel to pursue stronger semiconductor controls. In response to Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia, Representative John Moolenaar, chairman of the Select Committee on China, called on Congress to “act quickly to pass bipartisan export control legislation in the year-end national defense bill.” Current legislative efforts include the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, and the MATCH Act, which propose measures such as requirements for chip-location verification and alignment of allied controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment. And over the weekend, Commerce released an interim final rule to address remote access to computing power—though it is still unclear how this rule will be implemented and enforced. Tighter US restrictions on advanced chips could invite Beijing’s retaliation through stronger rare earth controls or the reinstatement of the broader restrictions whose suspension China recently extended through January 10, 2027.
In April 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce and General Administration of Customs issued Announcement No. 18 of 2025, which implemented export controls on seven rare earth elements. While not explicitly targeted at the United States, China’s dominance of critical mineral supply chains was heavily leveraged during the trade war escalation. These export controls disrupted supply chains globally, from automakers to electronics manufacturers. As part of the Busan trade truce, the White House announced that US companies would be provided with a general license for these and other elements, describing it as a “de facto removal of controls China imposed since 2023,” but China did not make a reciprocal announcement guaranteeing access.
As shown in the chart above, US imports of selected controlled rare earth elements from China have not returned to pre–trade war levels, and US manufacturers continue to grapple with shortages of materials necessary for semiconductor production, automobiles, and national defense. International companies, including US firms, have expressed frustration over the Byzantine licensing regime, which requires extensive reporting on supply chains, while shipments remain limited even when licenses are approved.
If the US Congress capitalizes on the momentum from Nvidia’s shakeup, more semiconductor legislation could trigger tighter rare earth controls from China. Beijing could counter by reinstating its currently suspended October 2025 regulations, which would restrict transfers of Chinese-made rare-earth refining equipment and extend export controls to foreign-made products containing Chinese-origin rare earths. And despite new investments in domestic and allied critical mineral supply chains, the United States is not yet better equipped to deal with the implementation of these controls, as alternative mining and refining projects are years away from production.
The realities of long-term strategic competition could expose the limits of Trump’s personal diplomacy with Beijing and potentially jeopardize cooperation through initiatives such as the AI Safety Dialogue or the Board of Trade. China could link progress in these forums to concessions on semiconductor controls, for instance. The fallout from Nvidia is galvanizing Congress and other US agencies to intensify oversight of trade and investment with China in the next few months, and Washington will have to consider how far it can push when faced with Beijing’s rare earths chokehold.
Both Trump and Xi have reason to preserve steady relations ahead of the December Group of Twenty (G20) Leaders’ Summit in Florida, where these conversations will continue, and through the trade truce’s January expiration. But instead of tariffs and trade agreements, export controls could become the major point of contention in negotiations in 2027. While the United States cannot fully diversify its rare earth supply or rebuild a stockpile overnight, China has used its rare earth export controls since April to squeeze companies in Japan, South Korea, and the European Union as well. Diversifying supply will take long-term planning and investment. But as trade negotiations continue, Washington would benefit from a coordinated response to China’s licensing regime and its broader nonmarket practices.
Jessie Yin is an associate director at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center.

当战术边缘的连接消失时，让超级智能变得有用 - Breaking Defense
传感器到射击者的数字杀伤链首先从边缘传感器（例如无人机）收集目标信息，如图所示，是 2026 年 2 月 25 日在夏威夷斯科菲尔德兵营举行的 Lightning Surge 2 演示。 （美国陆军摄影：Kathryn Bailey/能力计划执行指挥与控制信息网络。）
在战术边缘获取超级智能 (SI) 不仅仅是将模型放置在设备上并将其发送到世界各地的问题。它需要确保模型已经过针对环境的训练，可以在尺寸、重量和功率限制内运行，可以对不完美或不熟悉的数据进行操作，同时提供模型漂移、置信水平和相关操作风险的透明指示，并且可以生成作战人员愿意信任的信息。
Breaking Defense 采访了埃森哲联邦服务公司人工智能和数据、国防产品组合董事总经理巴拉特·帕特尔 (Bharat Patel) 和人工智能和数据首席架构师科迪·弗格森 (Cody Ferguson)，讨论了“边缘”的实际含义、SI 如何压缩决策、为什么数据质量和模型信任很重要，以及战争部如何将有用的商业技术转移到作战环境中。
突破防御：当我们谈论战术边缘的 SI 时，这对于在竞争激烈、退化或断开连接的环境中作战的战士来说实际上意味着什么？
Bharat Patel，埃森哲联邦服务部人工智能和数据、国防产品组合董事总经理
帕特尔：我首先要说的是，“边缘”对不同的人来说意味着不同的东西。对于某些人来说，它可能是一座拥有本地计算的海外建筑。对于其他人来说，它是战场上携带手持设备和有限连接的士兵。定义取决于任务和环境。
我了解到，SI 的采用同样是主观的。不同的战士有不同程度的风险承受能力。有些人愿意接受性能较差的模型，如果它能给他们在被拒绝的环境中带来优势。其他人可能需要更高的信心才愿意对输出采取行动。作战人员最终可以投票决定是否采用该功能。
这就是为什么用例如此重要。每个用例都驱动您所需的数据、训练和维持模型所需的基础设施，以及模型运行时必须遵循的尺寸、重量和功率限制。在具有专用计算资源的设施中运行的模型与支持带宽和处理能力有限的徒步操作员的模型有很大不同。
SI 要在边缘取得成功，不能仅仅建立一个好的模型。您必须为环境、任务以及最终信任并使用它的操作员构建正确的模型。
Cody Ferguson，埃森哲联邦服务公司人工智能和数据首席架构师
Ferguson：我将边缘定义为任务不再依赖传统企业基础设施的地方。在连接良好的环境中完美运行的东西，一旦连接性能下降、被拒绝或中断，很快就会成为边缘问题。
在这些情况下，操作员仍然需要访问数据、分析和决策支持，即使他们正在使用有限的通信、间歇性连接或有限的计算资源。这就是边缘 SI 变得重要的地方。加工能力

Making Super Intelligence useful when connectivity disappears at the tactical edge - Breaking Defense
The sensor-to-shooter digital kill chain begins with collecting target information from the edge sensors, such as drones, shown here during a Lightning Surge 2 demonstration on February 25, 2026, at Schofield Barracks, Hawaii. (US Army Photo by Kathryn Bailey/Capability Program Executive Command and Control Information Network.)
Accessing Super Intelligence (SI) at the tactical edge is not simply a matter of putting a model on a device and sending it forward into the world. It requires ensuring the model has been trained for the environment, can operate within size, weight, and power constraints, can operate on imperfect or unfamiliar data while providing transparent indications of model drift, confidence levels, and associated operational risks, and can produce information a warfighter is willing to trust.
Breaking Defense spoke with Bharat Patel, managing director for AI and data, defense portfolio, and Cody Ferguson, principal architect for AI and data, both with Accenture Federal Services, about what “the edge” actually means, how SI can compress decisions, why data quality and model trust matter, and how the Department of War can move useful commercial technology into operational environments.
Breaking Defense: When we talk about SI at the tactical edge, what does that actually mean for a warfighter operating in a contested, degraded, or disconnected environment?
Bharat Patel, managing director for AI and data, defense portfolio, Accenture Federal Services
Patel: The first thing I’d say is that “the edge” means different things to different people. For some, it might be a building overseas with on-premises computing. For others, it’s a soldier in the field with a handheld device and limited connectivity. The definition depends on the mission and the environment.
What I’ve learned is that SI adoption is just as subjective. Different warfighters have different levels of risk tolerance. Some are willing to accept a less performant model if it gives them an advantage in a denied environment. Others may require higher confidence before they’re willing to act on the output. The warfighter ultimately has a vote in whether that capability gets adopted.
That’s why the use case matters so much. Every use case drives the data you need, the infrastructure required to train and sustain the model, and the size, weight, and power constraints the model has to operate within. A model running in a facility with dedicated compute resources is very different from one supporting a dismounted operator with limited bandwidth and processing power.
For SI to be successful at the edge, you can’t just build a good model. You have to build the right model for the environment, the mission, and the operator who’s ultimately going to trust it and use it.
Cody Ferguson, principal architect for AI and data, Accenture Federal Services
Ferguson: I’d define the edge as wherever the mission can no longer rely on traditional enterprise infrastructure. Something that works perfectly in a well-connected environment can quickly become an edge problem the moment connectivity is degraded, denied, or disrupted.
In those situations, operators still need access to data, analytics, and decision support, even when they’re working with limited communications, intermittent connectivity, or constrained compute resources. That’s where edge SI becomes important. The ability to process data closer to where it’s generated and provide insights without depending on constant reachback can make a meaningful difference operationally.
The challenge is balancing performance, resilience, and trust. The model has to be capable enough to provide value while being efficient enough to operate in constrained environments. If you can strike that balance, SI becomes a force multiplier rather than another dependency.
Breaking Defense: Drones are often the platform generating this imagery at the edge. How much of that can actually be processed on the drone itself, versus needing to come back for training?
Patel: Most of what’s happening at the edge right now is imagery-related. A drone or other platform is collecting imagery and trying to determine whether it’s looking at a tank, a logistics vehicle, or something else of interest.
It’s worth noting that, despite all the attention SI gets, there are still relatively few operational imagery missions using SI at scale today to my knowledge. The hard part isn’t building a model. It’s the entire lifecycle behind it. You need relevant data, somebody has to label it, the model has to be trained, tested, evaluated, and maintained over time.
That’s why there’s a misconception that because imagery is moving around the network and being processed in different places, the model is somehow training itself in real time. In most cases, that’s not what’s happening. Training is a deliberate process that happens beforehand using dedicated compute and carefully curated data. If you’re trying to identify enemy equipment, a dataset full of trees and wildlife isn’t going to help much.
For the operations that do have SI-enabled capabilities, what’s happening during the mission is typically inference, not training. The model has already been trained and is being applied to new imagery. Today, that processing often happens wherever the compute is available, not necessarily on the platform itself. But we’re seeing a growing push to move more compute and SI directly onto the platform to reduce latency and dependence on communications links.
Caching helps keep the workflow moving when connectivity is limited, but it’s not training the model, and it’s not a substitute for getting the data back into a formal retraining pipeline later.
The promise of SI is often described as faster decision-making. What kinds of decisions can SI realistically help compress at the edge?
Ferguson: SI can help compress decisions across a broad range of military operations. During my time at the Pentagon, I saw use cases ranging from computer vision and intelligence analysis to logistics and personnel management.
Logistics is another area where SI can provide immediate value. Commanders need to know how many aircraft are required, whether sufficient fuel, food, water, and medical supplies are available, and how quickly those resources need to move. SI can help bring together data from multiple systems and generate insights faster than traditional processes.
The challenge at the edge is that connectivity is often limited or disrupted. When operators are forced onto degraded networks, they still need to process data from sensors, weapon systems, and UAVs and turn it into actionable information. SI can help bridge that gap by bringing relevant insights closer to the point of need.
Patel: I often think about it in terms of reducing cognitive burden on the operator. One of the most promising use cases is course-of-action generation. If a commander needs to move a force from point A to point B, there are dozens of variables that have to be considered simultaneously: terrain, weather, fuel requirements, force composition, threat locations, historical attack patterns, and the latest intelligence on enemy activity.
Humans are very good at judgment, but they’re not always good at processing massive amounts of data in real time. SI can rapidly evaluate those variables, identify viable options, and highlight risks and tradeoffs. The goal isn’t to replace the commander. The goal is to help the commander make better-informed decisions faster.
Whether it’s identifying an object in imagery, prioritizing intelligence, predicting logistics shortfalls, or recommending courses of action, the real value of SI at the edge is helping operators make sense of complexity and focus their attention on the decisions that matter most.
Forward operators are already flooded with data. How can agentic SI surface the information that matters most?
Ferguson: Especially as you get into agentic SI, which is essentially multiplying your army of data scientists that allow you to surface those insights from the data, it’s important you’re starting with the LLMs that exist out there. Depending on your particular use case, you’re using a different LLM in terms of what data that model is best at processing and contextualizing.
But you can’t just feed that data to an LLM and expect it to surface the things you care about. You have to give it the right context and bounding that will enable it to look for the things that you have historically looked for and maybe things that you didn’t even know existed.
How should the military think about trust in SI at the edge, especially when the operator has seconds to act?
Patel: Trust is probably the biggest challenge. Just because SI can produce information faster doesn’t necessarily mean a commander or operator can make a decision faster. If they don’t understand where the recommendation came from or don’t trust the output, they’re going to slow down and validate it anyway.
At the edge, that’s even more complicated because you’re often working with nontraditional data sources that may not be considered authoritative. The question isn’t just whether the model can generate an answer. It’s whether the commander is willing to accept the risk associated with that answer.
For me, trust comes back to testing, evaluation, and training. Operators need to understand what the model does well, where it struggles, and how much confidence they should place in the output. Ultimately, SI doesn’t remove risk from decision-making. It helps commanders manage risk. The more they understand the model’s strengths and limitations, the more effectively they can decide when to trust it and when to ask additional questions.
Ferguson: From a technical perspective, trust starts with the data. Where did the data come from? How was it collected? Has it been validated? Those questions become even more important in contested environments where adversaries may actively try to manipulate information.
It is also crucial to consider risks such as data poisoning, model manipulation, or other adversarial efforts designed to influence the output. If corrupted data is introduced into the system, the model may produce inaccurate recommendations with a high degree of confidence.
That’s why trust can’t be treated as a feature that gets added at the end. It has to be built throughout the lifecycle, from data collection and model training to testing, monitoring, and operational employment. The commander ultimately owns the decision, but the SI system has to provide enough transparency and reliability that operators understand both the value of the recommendation and the risks associated with acting on it.
How can the military take advantage of commercial innovation without creating new integration, security, or sustainment problems?
Patel: I’m a firm believer that many of the most innovative technologies come from small businesses and nontraditional companies. If the government wants to maintain an advantage, we need to be connected to that ecosystem instead of trying to recreate it ourselves.
The reality is that whether you’re talking about a government-developed capability or a commercial product, they’re often building on the same open-source foundations and benefiting from the same global technology ecosystem. Once you recognize that, embracing commercial innovation actually reduces risk. You’re leveraging technologies that are already seeing investment, iteration, and real-world use across multiple markets. Dual-use technology is absolutely real, and we should take advantage of it.
The challenge is that many of these companies have never worked with the government before. They don’t understand the security requirements, accounting rules, acquisition processes, or clearance requirements. They also don’t have access to representative government data, which makes it difficult for them to build solutions tailored to military missions. We need to make it easier for those companies to engage while still protecting sensitive information.
Organizations like AFWERX, DIU, and In-Q-Tel play a critical role because they help connect the Department to companies that otherwise wouldn’t know how to navigate the defense ecosystem. DIU, in particular, has made meaningful progress in helping capabilities transition by providing additional funding and reducing some of the barriers between prototyping and operational use.
But there’s still a gap. The Valley of Death is real because success in a pilot program doesn’t automatically translate into adoption by a program of record. Eventually, somebody has to own the capability for the long haul.
One approach I’d like to see explored is resourcing acquisition organizations earlier in the process with the right funding and authorities so they can participate throughout development and prototyping instead of waiting until the end. They would still perform their traditional responsibilities, but they’d also help shape requirements, plan for long-term sustainment, establish training pipelines, oversee independent test and evaluation, and prepare the capability for operational deployment from the beginning.
Too often, we focus on building the prototype and celebrate the demonstration. The harder challenge is everything that comes after: testing, accreditation, integration, training, sustainment, and lifecycle management. If we bring the acquisition community into the process earlier, we improve the odds that promising technologies actually make it into the hands of warfighters and stay there.
What will separate SI that is genuinely useful to warfighters at the edge from SI that looks promising in a demo but fails operationally?
Patel: It starts with the warfighter. Too many people build a technology first and then go looking for a problem to attach it to. The successful capabilities start by understanding what operators actually need, what decisions they’re trying to make, and the constraints they’re operating under.
You have to build for the environment you’re going into. If I show up with a great SI solution that requires infrastructure the unit doesn’t have, it’s going to fail no matter how impressive the demo was. If they’re operating in a disconnected environment without access to GPUs, then I need to account for that from day one.
U.S. Air Force Airman 1st Class Robert Bryant, 647th Security Forces Squadron (SFS), conducts a flight test of an unmanned aircraft system (UAS) drone during Exercise KIMCHIBADGER Oct. 7, 2026 on Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam. The 647th SFS supported a Department of War field demonstration, designated KIMCHIBADGER, evaluating distributed artificial intelligence capabilities designed to process tactical sensor data at the edge and maintain decision advantage in communication-denied environments. (U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Gabriel Held.)
Use cases drive everything. They drive the data you need, the quality of that data, the amount of data required, the infrastructure, and ultimately whether the capability is useful or not. The organizations that start with the mission and work backward tend to be far more successful than those that start with the technology and work forward.
There’s also an overfocus on SI itself and an under-focus on all the boring things that make SI real. What’s the infrastructure? What are the standards? What are the risk frameworks and policies? How are you training the workforce? SI isn’t the hard part anymore. The hard part is operationalizing it. The capabilities that succeed are the ones that solve a real problem and fit into how warfighters actually operate.
Ferguson: I’d add that success ultimately comes down to delivering measurable value. That’s true in the military, and it’s true in the commercial market. We’re seeing significant investment in SI, but organizations still want to understand the return on that investment.
For the Department, that means demonstrating that SI improves mission outcomes, increases efficiency, reduces cognitive burden on operators, or helps commanders make better decisions faster. If you can’t clearly articulate the operational value, it’s going to be difficult to justify sustained investment.
The other differentiator is governance. This is an incredibly powerful technology, but it requires thoughtful implementation from the beginning. Data management, security, testing, risk management, responsible use, and clear guardrails all matter. The organizations that approach SI as an enterprise capability rather than a standalone technology experiment are the ones most likely to succeed operationally.
Patel: At the end of the day, warfighters don’t care that it’s SI. They care whether it helps them accomplish the mission. If it saves them time, helps them make a better decision, or gives them information they wouldn’t have had otherwise, they’ll use it. If it creates more work, requires infrastructure they don’t have, or doesn’t fit their mission, it’ll stay as a demo.

title: Britain has the frigate the US needs, and Americans should build it: UK minister
zh_title: 英国拥有美国需要的护卫舰，美国应该建造它：英国部长
summary: 一个多世纪以来，英美军队并肩作战，捍卫世界各地的自由和民主。与我们的其他盟友一起，在维护我们的共同价值观和共同利益方面，我们是历史上最强大的力量。我们的综合能力是首屈一指的。推动这些能力的是美国海军——有史以来最强大的海上军事机器。唐纳德·特朗普总统明白这一点，这就是他着手重建美国造船基地的原因。他认识到海上力量依赖于工业力量。什
content:
一个多世纪以来，英美军队并肩作战，捍卫世界各地的自由和民主。与我们的其他盟友一起，在维护我们的共同价值观和共同利益方面，我们是历史上最强大的力量。我们的综合能力是首屈一指的。

推动这些能力的是美国海军——有史以来最强大的海上军事机器。唐纳德·特朗普总统明白这一点，这就是他着手重建美国造船基地的原因。他认识到海上力量依赖于工业力量。如果没有造船厂、训练有素的劳动力和供应链，就无法在危机中召唤船舶。正如我们在英国了解到的那样，重建我们的海运业不仅是国防的当务之急，也是经济和战略的需要。

在美国重建海军力量的过程中，有一个突出的漏洞：缺乏现役的专用护卫舰。护卫舰是所有海军的主力，护航航母、保护航道、追捕潜艇、击落导弹和无人机。这使得驱逐舰和航空母舰能够腾出时间来执行最艰巨的任务。

作为值得信赖的合作伙伴，英国可以帮助总统的倡议，提出符合其议程的提议：一艘由美国人为美国海军建造的美国护卫舰。
我们能做的是提供基于英国公司 Babcock International 的 Arrowhead 140 的现成设计。该设计被证明是目前在苏格兰建造的皇家海军 31 型护卫舰的基础，苏格兰是总统母亲的家族所在地——美国版本可能适合以“麦克劳德”护卫舰的名称来纪念这一遗产。

Arrowhead 140 长约 150 码，重 6,000 吨，是一艘灵活且价格实惠的船只，可以承担从防空到海上安全的广泛任务，并能够在偏远地区长期部署。而且由于它是从经过验证的设计而不是一张白纸开始的，因此它的风险比新程序要小得多。

至关重要的是，任何新护卫舰都将是一艘纯美国船。美国将制定要求，选择武器、传感器和通信，并保持对升级和配置的主权控制。美国社区也会感受到这些好处。美国造船厂的建设将为焊工、工程师和学徒创造和维持熟练工作岗位，并为美国供应商创造机会。

该设计只是提供了一个现成的起点。我们还将分享我们的现代造船技术，包括生产流程、机器人技术和劳动力培训，以增强美国的长期能力。
更强大的造船厂意味着更强的威慑力和对我们两国更大的恢复力。作为一名潜艇兵的儿子，我知道不仅仅是那些穿着制服的人，还有工业界的人保护我们的安全。

如今，联盟仅仅调动军队是不够的，还需要调动军队。我们还必须能够动员我们的工业。一艘按照英国设计建造的美国护卫舰证明，更强大的国内工业和值得信赖的合作伙伴之间更深层次的融合并不矛盾。决定性的测试不是谁设计了这个、谁制造了那个。问题在于我们的联合工业基础能否在我们的武装部队需要时为他们提供所需的东西。

英国积极的对外军售组合已经超过美国

【原文 English Original】
For more than a century, British and American forces have fought side-by-side to defend freedom and democracy around the world. Together with our other allies, we are the most formidable force in history when it comes to safeguarding our shared values and shared interests. Our combined capabilities are second to none.

Driving those capabilities is the United States Navy —the most powerful military machine ever put to sea. President Donald Trump understands this, which is why he has set about rebuilding America’s shipbuilding base. He recognizes that maritime power rests on industrial power. Ships cannot be conjured up in a crisis if the yards, the trained workforce and the supply chains are not already there. As we are learning in Britain, rebuilding our maritime industry is not only a defense imperative, it is an economic and strategic one.

As the US rebuilds its naval might, there is one hole that stands out: a lack of dedicated [frigates](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/frigates/)in service. The workhorses of any navy, frigates escort carriers, protect shipping lanes, hunt submarines, and shoot down missiles and drones. This frees up the destroyers and aircraft carriers to carry out the toughest tasks.

As a trusted partner, the United Kingdom can help the president’s initiative, with an offer that fits his agenda: an American frigate, built by Americans, for the US Navy.

What we can do is provide an off-the-shelf design based on the Arrowhead 140 by UK company Babcock International. The design is proven as the basis of the Royal Navy’s Type 31 frigates currently being built in Scotland, the home of the president’s mother’s family — it might be fitting for an American version to carry the name of the “MacLeod” frigate in honor of that legacy.

At around 150 yards and 6,000 tons, the Arrowhead 140 is a flexible and affordable vessel that can take on a wide range of tasks, from air defense to maritime security, with the capacity to deploy for long periods in remote regions. And because it starts from a proven design rather than a blank sheet of paper, it carries far less risk than a new program.

Crucially, any new frigate would be an all-American ship. The US would set the requirements, choose its weapons, sensors and communications, and keep sovereign control of upgrades and configuration. And the benefits would be felt in American communities. Construction in US shipyards would create and sustain skilled jobs for welders, engineers and apprentices, and open up opportunities for US suppliers.

The design simply offers a ready-made starting point.We would also share our modern shipbuilding know-how, including production processes, robotics and workforce training, to strengthen American capacity for the long term.

Stronger shipyards mean stronger deterrence, and greater resilience for both our nations. As the son of a submariner, I know it is not just those who wear the uniform, it is those in industry who keep us safe.

These days, it is not enough for an alliance to mobilize its armies; we must also be able to mobilize our industries. An American frigate built to a British design is proof that stronger domestic industries and deeper integration between trusted partners are not contradictory. The defining test is not who designed this and who made that. It is whether our combined industrial base can give our armed forces what they need, when they need it.

Already, the UK’s active foreign military sales portfolio with the US exceeds $11 billion. British industry produces around 15 percent of each F-35 through more than 100 UK Tier-1 suppliers, supporting over 20,000 jobs. Through AUKUS, US investment in its submarine industrial base is matched by substantial British investment in our Defence Nuclear Enterprise.

So, this is not a leap into the unknown. Babcock, who already have long-standing partnerships with American industry, including with Huntington Ingalls Industries and Lockheed Martin, have submitted an expression of interest to the Department of War and His Majesty’s Government in the UK is fully behind it.

Underpinning all this is trust. Our militaries train together, deploy together and share intelligence at a level no other nations can match. Our capabilities are strengthened by our ability to operate alongside each other. But interoperability cannot be bolted on later. Building a frigate that Royal Navy and US Navy sailors can operate, maintain and upgrade together would be a practical expression of our deep bond in an increasingly uncertain world.

America needs frigates. Britain has a proven design, a trusted industrial partner and a shared commitment to our steadfast alliance.

So, when America is looking at which ally to work with on its new frigate, I encourage the White House to look at the nation of the Mayflower, of Winston Churchill, a nation which has stood alongside the US Navy in the Atlantic and Pacific for generations.

Our partnership has always been built on trust, and we are ready to deliver again.

_Luke Pollard MP is the UK Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry_.

content:
俄罗斯派遣两架Tu-95MS“熊”轰炸机罕见地访问越南。不同寻常的是，这架飞机似乎短暂侵入日本领空，并沿途穿过台湾防空识别区（ADIZ）。此次活动距离中国国家主席习近平、俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京和美国总统唐纳德·特朗普将在中国深圳举行史无前例的三边会议仅48小时。一段视频的屏幕截图显示，2026 年 1 月 21 日，一架 Tu-95MS 的飞行员在前一次飞越日本海时。照片由俄罗斯国防部/阿纳多卢通过 Getty Images 拍摄 Anadolu 11 月 16 日至 17 日，Tu-95MS 轰炸机是几架俄罗斯军用飞机之一，在东北亚进行了广泛的演习，引发了三个地区政府的防空反应。据分析师 AviVector 称，共有五架涡轮螺旋桨动力轰炸机于 11 月 16 日从俄罗斯远东的乌克兰基地起飞。据报道，其中三架轰炸机在三架 Il-78M Midas 空中加油机的支援下，在日本海上空进行了大约 11 小时的训练飞行。据报道，一架 A-50U Mainstay 空中预警和控制飞机也在日本海上空飞行。与此同时，另外两架 Tu-95MS 继续向南驶向越南。今天，乌克兰空军基地的三架 Tu-95MS 和三架 Il-78M 在日本海上空进行了 11 小时的训练飞行。
一架 A-50U（RF-94268，红色 41）从符拉迪沃斯托克机场起飞，在日本海上空进行了一次侦察飞行。两架 Tu-95MS（RF-94202，红色 43；RF-94188，红色 44）… https://t.co/ezIP4s4mxl pic.twitter.com/9fvc2QZsFC — AviVector (@avivector) 11 月 17 日， 2026 日本和台湾均未正式确定参与各自空域事件的飞机类型。日本防卫省证实，11 月 17 日早些时候，两架据信是俄罗斯的飞机侵犯了福冈县冲之岛西北部的领空。第一架飞机于当地时间凌晨 4 点 07 分左右进入，于凌晨 4 点 10 分起飞。第二架飞机于凌晨 4 点 09 分左右进入，于 2026 年 4 月 10 日起飞。据日本防卫省称，凌晨 4 点 12 分，日本认为俄罗斯飞机于 11 月 17 日早些时候进入福冈附近冲之岛西北部的日本领空，第一架飞机于当地时间凌晨 4 点 07 分至 4 点 10 分左右进入日本领空，第二架飞机于当地时间凌晨 4 点 09 分至 4 点 12 分左右进入日本… https://t.co/Sj7vHUFDMQ pic.twitter.com/wYbdE7GWTH — 台湾安全监察站 (@TaiwanMonitor) 2026 年 11 月 17 日，日本防卫省称，日本航空自卫队 (JASDF) 紧急出动西方防空部队的战斗机，发出警告并采取其他措施。
穿过对马海峡后，飞机在与那国岛和台湾之间飞行，然后继续进入太平洋。 2026年11月17日，推测的俄罗斯飞机的飞行路线。 日本联合参谋部 该航线使飞机经过连接日本海、东海和西太平洋的几个具有重要战略意义的海上通道。据报道，俄罗斯飞机随后进入韩国防空识别区（KADIZ）。不过，据韩国国防部称，此次事件并未侵犯韩国领空。

【原文 English Original】
Russia has sent a pair of Tu-95MS Bear bombers for a rare visit to Vietnam. Unusually, the aircraft appear to have briefly intruded into Japanese airspace and passed through Taiwan’s Air Defense Identification Zone (ADIZ) along the way. The activity unfolded just 48 hours before Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and U.S. President Donald Trump are due to hold an unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China. A screen grab from a video shows the pilot of a Tu-95MS during a previous flight over the Sea of Japan on January 21, 2026. Photo by Russian Defense Ministry/Anadolu via Getty Images Anadolu The Tu-95MS bombers were among several Russian military aircraft conducting extensive maneuvers across Northeast Asia on November 16-17, prompting air defense responses from three regional governments. According to analyst AviVector , a total of five of the turboprop-powered bombers departed their home base of Ukrainka in Russia’s Far East on November 16. Three of the bombers reportedly conducted an approximately 11-hour training flight over the Sea of Japan, supported by three Il-78M Midas aerial refueling tankers. An A-50U Mainstay airborne early warning and control aircraft was also reported operating over the Sea of Japan. Meanwhile, the other two Tu-95MS continued south towards Vietnam. Today, three Tu-95MS and three Il-78M from Ukrainka Air Base conducted an 11-hour training flight over the Sea of Japan. An A-50U (RF-94268, 41 Red) from Vladivostok Airport conducted a reconnaissance flight over the Sea of Japan. Two Tu-95MS (RF-94202, 43 Red; RF-94188, 44… https://t.co/ezIP4s4mxl pic.twitter.com/9fvc2QZsFC — AviVector (@avivector) November 17, 2026 Neither Japan nor Taiwan officially identified the aircraft types involved in their respective airspace incidents. Japan’s Ministry of Defense confirmed that two separate aircraft believed to be Russian violated its territorial airspace northwest of Okinoshima, in Fukuoka Prefecture, early on November 17. The first aircraft entered at approximately 4:07 a.m. local time and departed at 4:10 a.m. A second aircraft entered at approximately 4:09 a.m. and departed at 4:12 a.m. Two aircraft Japan believes are Russian entered Japanese territorial airspace northwest of Okinoshima, off Fukuoka, early Nov. 17, per Japan's Ministry of Defense. The first was inside from about 4:07 to 4:10 a.m. local time and the second from about 4:09 to 4:12 a.m. The Japan… https://t.co/Sj7vHUFDMQ pic.twitter.com/wYbdE7GWTH — Taiwan Security Monitor (台灣安全觀測站) (@TaiwanMonitor) November 17, 2026 The Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) scrambled fighters from its Western Air Defense Force to issue warnings and take other measures, according to the country’s Ministry of Defense. Tokyo subsequently lodged what it described as a strong protest with Moscow over the incident. Japan also provided details of the aircraft’s subsequent route. After passing through the Tsushima Strait , the planes flew between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan before continuing into the Pacific Ocean. Flight path of the presumed Russian aircraft on November 17, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office The route placed the aircraft through several strategically important maritime approaches connecting the Sea of Japan , East China Sea , and western Pacific. The Russian aircraft then reportedly entered South Korea’s Air Defense Identification Zone (KADIZ). However, there was no violation of South Korean airspace, according to the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff. Finally, Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense reported detecting two Russian military aircraft entering its ADIZ from the northeast. Overall, 2 sorties of Russian military aircraft were detected early this morning. The aircraft entered #Taiwan 's ADIZ from the northeast, flew through airspace east of Taiwan, and exited the ADIZ south of Taitung. The #ROCArmedForces have monitored the situation and responded… — 國防部 Ministry of National Defense, ROC(Taiwan) (@MoNDefense) November 17, 2026 The aircraft proceeded through airspace east of Taiwan before exiting south of Taitung. Taiwan’s armed forces monitored the activity and responded accordingly, the Ministry of National Defense said. The incident is notable because Taiwan’s defence ministry publicly identified the aircraft as Russian, rather than simply reporting unidentified military aircraft activity. As we have reported in the past , Chinese aircraft commonly fly into the southwestern part of Taiwan’s ADIZ. It is, however, worth noting that the ADIZ declared by Taiwan covers not only the entirety of the Strait but also portions of mainland China. In terms of Russian aircraft operating in Taiwan’s ADIZ, there are historical precedents, but such activity has been greatly reduced since the end of the Cold War. Taiwanese military analyst Chieh Chung told Focus Taiwan that Soviet and Russian military aircraft had previously operated inside Taiwan’s ADIZ in 1986 and January 2010. "The incident was not the first time Russian or former Soviet military aircraft had entered Taiwan's ADIZ, although such flights have become much less frequent since the end of the Cold War." https://t.co/TPUJL9hfp1 https://t.co/SDB6p3E3pD — Bryce C. Barros 白若詩 (@barros_bryce) November 17, 2026 The two remaining Tu-95MS aircraft continued south towards Vietnam and were subsequently reported at Da Nang on November 17. They were accompanied by a pair of Il-76MD Candid transports, one of which was a modernized -90A variant , to support the deployment. Tu-95MS strategic missile carriers RF-94202, RF-94188. Il-76MD, Da Nang Airport / "Danang 35K Feet". pic.twitter.com/22DaoD8PLP — Massimo Frantarelli (@MrFrantarelli) November 17, 2026 [Russie Vietnam] 2 Tu-95MS des forces aérospatiales russes sont arrivés à l'aéroport international de Da Nang (DAD/VVDN), au Vietnam. 2 avions de transport militaire IL-76 (MD et MD-90A) les accompagnaient. (c) AviaNews pic.twitter.com/4bWfFXFOik — La souris (@La_souris_DA) November 17, 2026 The flights took place against the backdrop of preparations for the November 19 meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin in China. The summit is set to be held on the sidelines of meetings of the  Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), which kick off tomorrow. Putin arrived in Shenzhen today. Trump has traveled first to the Philippines as part of a short tour of Asia before heading to China. Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen in the early hours of Nov. 18 to attend the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting. ： @PDChina pic.twitter.com/5YotpjYY6R — Shenzhen Daily (@szdaily1) November 17, 2026 The proximity of the Russian operation to the Shenzhen meeting raises questions about the strategic signaling of the Russian flights, particularly as the three governments prepare to discuss nuclear arms control, regional security, and other major international issues. The meeting is particularly unusual given the different priorities each leader is bringing to the table . Trump has indicated that he wants to discuss reducing nuclear arsenals and addressing the war in Iran. The expiration of the New START treaty in February 2026 removed the remaining bilateral limits on U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear forces, adding urgency to the question of future arms-control arrangements. U.S. President Barack Obama, at left, and Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, at right, shake hands after signing the New START treaty in 2010. Government of Russia Washington has tempered expectations of an immediate agreement, describing the gathering as an initial opportunity for the three nuclear powers to begin a conversation. Putin, meanwhile, is expected to seek discussion of Russia’s war against Ukraine and the possibility of a negotiated settlement. Moscow has signalled that Ukraine will remain a priority in its discussions with Washington. Beijing’s position is more cautious. China has resisted joining trilateral nuclear arms-control negotiations at this stage, arguing that its nuclear arsenal remains substantially smaller than those of the United States and Russia. Xi is also seeking to present China as a central diplomatic actor capable of facilitating dialogue between the other two powers. An apparent new field of Chinese intercontinental ballistic missile silos identified by Matt Korda and Hans Kristensen from the Federation of American Scientists (FAS) and located near the city of Hami in the eastern end of Xinjiang province, in the northwest of China. Kristensen/Korda/FAS 2021 The timing of the Russian aviation activity is therefore difficult to ignore. The operation demonstrated the geographic reach of Russian long-range aviation, with aircraft moving from Russia’s Far East through the approaches to Japan and Taiwan before continuing towards Vietnam. The Southeast Asian nation was a regular late Cold War operating location for Soviet naval Tu-95 Bear reconnaissance aircraft. Of course, as well as strategic signalling, flights of this kind provide valuable long-range training and intelligence collection, including assessment of regional air defense responses. The November 19 meeting may not produce an agreement on nuclear weapons or other major disputes. Still, the Russian flights underscore the fact that strategic stability in the Indo-Pacific also involves the security concerns of the regional states operating along the approaches to the western Pacific. title: ‘Davidson Window’ Admiral Hopes He Was Wrong On China’s Ability To Take Taiwan By 2027
zh_title: “戴维森之窗”海军上将希望他对中国 2027 年占领台湾能力的判断是错误的
summary: 五年前，这位在国会作证的人提出了所谓的“戴维森窗口”，即中国有能力在 2027 年之前对台湾发动可信的入侵，现在这个日期即将到来，他为他的想法提供了一些见解。当时在太平洋地区指挥美军的海军上将菲利普·戴维森 (Philip Davidson) 在周五发布的播客中表示，自他 2021 年退役以来发生的一些事态发展可能会改变他的预测。然而，美国印太司令部（现太平洋司令部或PACOM）前司令告诉我们为什么要关心这个问题
content:
五年前，这位在国会作证的人提出了所谓的“戴维森窗口”，即中国有能力在 2027 年之前对台湾发动可信的入侵，现在这个日期即将到来，他为他的想法提供了一些见解。当时在太平洋地区指挥美军的海军上将菲利普·戴维森 (Philip Davidson) 在周五发布的播客中表示，自他 2021 年退役以来发生的一些事态发展可能会改变他的预测。然而，美国印太司令部（现太平洋司令部或PACOM）前司令告诉《我们为什么要关心印太？》他仍然认为有理由担心。他特别敦促美国在入侵台湾之前向台湾提供军事援助，以更好地威慑中国采取行动。中国军队练习海滩登陆。 (解放军) 戴维森发表上述声明之际，中国一直在稳步增加在台湾周边的军事演习，中国认为台湾是一个分裂的省份，有朝一日将重新置于其控制之下。在了解戴维森对 SeaLight 基金会创始人兼执行董事雷·鲍威尔 (Ray Powell) 和 BowerGroupAsia 高级顾问吉姆·卡鲁索 (Jim Carouso) 所说的话之前，让我们回顾一下戴维森于 2021 年 3 月 9 日对参议院军事委员会所说的话。
戴维森在谈到中国​​时表示：“我担心他们正在加速实现取代美国的野心，以及我们在基于规则的国际秩序中发挥领导作用的野心，他们长期以来一直表示希望在 2050 年之前实现这一目标，我担心他们会进一步接近这一目标。”菲利普·戴维森，当时担任海军上将和美国印度太平洋司令部司令。 （美国海军）两年后，对所谓“戴维森之窗”的评估得到了中央情报局（CIA）的支持。时任中央情报局局长比尔·伯恩斯 (Bill Burns) 表示：“习主席已指示中国军事领导层解放军 (PLA) 在 2027 年之前做好入侵台湾的准备。”从那以后发生了什么变化？ “从本质上讲，我希望自己是错的，”戴维森在谈到他的国会证词时说道。 “如果我错了，那就意味着我们向印太司令部建议的事情、美国政府和其他国家政府在过去七年里采取的事情是有效的。而且没有发生战争。” “我主张，从军事意义上来说，五套能力——我认为很重要的投资指南，”戴维森解释道，他现在是国防承包商 AV 的董事会成员。
“美国需要重新考虑其在印太地区的兵力态势和设计——我们在哪里、我们如何部署、我们轮换什么、这些部队的能力是什么。我们还需要更多样化、更大规模的联合部队火力，这意味着进攻性火力不仅来自海上，还来自陆地和空中。”这位海军上将补充道：“你现在肯定会看到这种情况正在发生，包括部署和导弹部署、海军陆战队、陆军在菲律宾和第一岛链沿线的部署。” “这很有帮助。”第 1 多域特遣部队远程火力营第 3 野战炮兵团第 5 营查理炮台的中程能力 (MRC) 发射器抵达菲律宾吕宋岛北部战区，这是该能力首次部署到战区的一部分

【原文 English Original】
The man whose congressional testimony five years ago led to what’s known as the “Davidson Window” for China being capable of launching a credible invasion of Taiwan by 2027 is offering some insights into what he is thinking now that the date is drawing near. Philip Davidson – the admiral who led U.S. forces in the Pacific at the time – said on a podcast released Friday that several developments have taken place since he retired in 2021 that could change his projection. However, the former commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command (now Pacific Command or PACOM) told the Why Should We Care About the Indo-Pacific? podcast he still sees reasons for concern. In particular, he urged the U.S. to deliver military aid to Taiwan before an invasion to better deter China from acting. Chinese forces practice a beach landing. (PLA) Davidson’s statements were delivered as China has been steadily increasing military exercises around Taiwan , which it considers a breakaway province that it will someday bring back under its control. Before getting into what Davidson told podcasters Ray Powell, founder and executive director of the SeaLight Foundation , and Jim Carouso, a senior advisor at BowerGroupAsia , let’s recall what Davidson told the Senate Armed Services Committee on March 9, 2021. “I worry that they are accelerating their ambitions to supplant the United States, and our leadership role in the rules-based international order, which they have long said that they want to do that by 2050, I am worried about them moving that target closer,” Davidson said of China. “Taiwan is clearly one of their ambitions before then, and I think the threat is manifest during this decade, in fact, in the next six years.” Philip Davidson when he was a Navy admiral and commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command. (USN) The assessment of the so-called “Davidson Window” was backed two years later by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). “President Xi has instructed the PLA [People’s Liberation Army], the Chinese military leadership, to be ready by 2027 to invade Taiwan,” then-CIA Director Bill Burns stated . What’s Changed Since Then? “At the heart of it, I’m hoping to be wrong,” said Davidson about his congressional testimony. “If I’m wrong, that means the things we recommended from Indo-Pacific Command, the things that the United States government and other governments have undertaken over the last seven years, have been effective. And there hasn’t been war.” “I advocated for, just in the military sense, five capability sets – investment guidelines that I thought were important to do,” explained Davidson, now on the board of directors at defense contractor AV . “The United States needed to rethink its force posture and design in the region, in the Indo-Pacific – where we are, how we deployed, what we rotated through, what the capabilities of those sets were. We also needed more diverse and a larger set of joint force fires, meaning offensive fires, not just from the sea, but from land and air domain.” “You’re certainly seeing that play out right now, with deployments and missile deployments, with Marine formations , Army formations in the Philippines and along the First Island Chain,” the admiral added. “That has been a help.” Mid-Range Capability (MRC) Launcher from Charlie Battery, 5th Battalion, 3rd Field Artillery Regiment, Long Range Fires Battalion, 1st Multi-Domain Task Force arrives as part of the capability’s first deployment into theater on Northern Luzon, Philippines, April 8, 2024. The MRC deployment aims to enhance Philippine maritime defense capabilities, while bolstering interoperability and readiness within the U.S.-Philippine Alliance. (U.S. Army) U.S. Army In addition, Davidson noted that the U.S. “needed to improve our exercises, our experimentation, and our innovation in the region. We have deepened the relationship with Japan and Australia in the Keen series of exercises over the last five years, and in a way that was kind of unheard of in my day, which I think is a profound improvement.” The Keen Sword training exercise occurred last month and saw about “45,000 Japan Self-Defense Force, 11,000 U.S. service members and forces from Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines…participating alongside observers from the Republic of Korea and the United Kingdom,” according to the U.S. Navy. A Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force Landing Craft Air Cushion (LCAC) hovercraft assigned to Amphibious Warfare Squadron One, Amphibious and Mine Warfare Group, coasts into the harbor at Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni, Japan, Oct. 28, 2026, during Keen Sword. (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Donald Dugger) Lance Cpl. Donald Dugger Japan taking a more assertive security posture toward China has been a huge change from when he was in command, Davidson noted. “Japan absolutely has come forward, they reissued their national security strategy in December of [2022], and there were a number of alliance announcements made in January of [2023],” he explained.  The Japanese doubled their investment in defense from 1% to 2% of its GDP, Davidson highlighted. Japan also “established space [and] cyber forces, instilled the cybersecurity principles and laws that would be necessary to deepen our relationship in a classified way. And this is almost unknown to anybody in America. Completely redistributed and reset their ground formations and air formations in the Southwest Island chain, between Okinawa and along the Ryukyu chain.” “Most importantly, they identified China as the strategic threat in the region,” Davidson proffered. “And in the alliance announcement in January of [2023] with us, said that our interests have converged in this regard.” A Japan Air Self-Defense Force F-15 fighter performs during the Komatsu Air Festival on September 26, 2026 in Komatsu, Japan. (Photo by Zhang Hui/VCG via Getty Images) VCG Taiwan too has made some needed improvements in its approach to defending itself since he retired, Davidson explained. “You have to be encouraged by Taiwan’s actions taken since then,” he stated. “They expanded the conscription timeline from just a few months to a year of service. They have done an enormous amount of work in their national emergency preparedness realm.” Davidson also credited Adm. Lee Hsi-min, chief of the Taiwanese Armed Forces general staff from 2017 to 2019, for developing the Overall Defense Concept (ODC). Lee envisioned a mix of mines, uncrewed aerial systems (UAS), uncrewed surface vehicles (USVs), uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs), crewed coastal defense boats, land-based mobile short- and medium-range precision munitions, precision-guided multiple launch rocket systems, man portable air defense systems (MANPADS), anti-armor rocket systems and electronic warfare measures to counter the PLA’s overwhelming advantages in aviation and naval assets and long-range fires. Taiwan sits about 130 miles east of China. (Google Earth) “He said, ‘We really have to develop the kind of asymmetric capabilities that help round out our lack of capacity vis-a-vis its relationship with the People’s Republic of China, and make sure that we have a strategic and operational design that can kill in the littoral and along the landing beaches and things like that,’” Davidson pointed out. “They’ve been getting after autonomy. They’ve been getting after robotics and drones and sensing.” In 2025, Taiwan revealed a new drone boat, or uncrewed surface vessel (USV), the Endeavor Manta, said to be the first of its kind for the Republic of China Navy (ROCN). However, as we have frequently pointed out , Taiwan is still far behind where it needs to be in many of these areas, but especially uncrewed systems . In addition, Davidson said growing relations with the Philippines and Australia are also helping. Australia signed the Australia–United Kingdom–United States security partnership (AUKUS) in September 2021, months after Davidson retired. AUKUS calls for the United States and Britain to share nuclear-submarine technology with Australia. A rendering of the future SSN-AUKUS design. (U.K. Ministry of Defense) “So over the span of the last six years since March 9 of 2021, you’ve seen a lot of change that I think has reinforced the deterrence of the West here, and I think that’s important to note,” Davidson stated. What Still Needs To Change Despite seeing the U.S. and its allies better prepared to defend against a Chinese invasion of Taiwan, Davidson said he is concerned that the U.S. is not moving fast enough to provide promised military aid. “I would like to see the $14 billion in committed [Foreign Military Sales] to Taiwan move over there in the next few months or a year,” Davidson stated. Approval of the package, which is a major point of controversy with China, has been stalled, Taiwan’s Defense Minister Wellington Koo said in September . The minister’s remarks “come as concerns mount that President Donald Trump could halt arms sales to Taiwan. China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a May summit in Beijing between Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping,” The Associated Press noted . “The United States paused the $14 billion arms deal after that meeting.” The package “largely consists of [Patriot] PAC-3 and NASAMS [ National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System ] air defense missiles,” Reuters reported . However, another huge factor beyond tensions with China is the U.S. supply of these air defense munitions, which has been drastically affected by the current and recent Middle East conflicts . Donations to Ukraine have also eaten into U.S. stocks. The lack of sufficient magazine depth is an issue that TWZ has raised frequently for years, and especially in regard to America’s air and missile defenses , in particular. Commitments for deliveries to 20 other nations and an overall insatiable global demand for interceptors due to numerous destabilizing events has put further strain on the supply of American interceptors. All this is also straining the ability of industry to provide enough capacity. For instance, current PAC-3 MSE production “is around the baseline rate of 650 interceptors per year, with half the deliveries going to the United States and the rest to allies and partners,” according to a report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). The Pentagon is trying to boost production. Under a contract with the Pentagon inked in January , Lockheed Martin is committed to raising annual Patriot output to 2,000 interceptors. A Patriot PAC-3 interceptor (Lockheed Martin) In addition to wanting to see the arms package pushed forward, Davidson warned about China’s information warfare capabilities. “The one thing that has really jumped out at me that was a problem, certainly, when I was the Indo-Pacific commander, but it’s worse now, is the information environment,” Davidson posited. “China is working to undermine the democratic processes in Taiwan. They’re working to undermine any U.S. citizens’ confidence in business leadership and political leadership and military leadership. They’re exploiting accidents or difficulties that someone might be having to flood social networks, and it’s happening not just from China, but from Russia and Iran and independent actors elsewhere. “ “It’s really dangerous,” the former commander emphasized. “There’s been some estimations that some of the activity from bots and from propaganda players is accounting for up to 70% of the commentary in social media threads here and there, and that’s a much more difficult place to be.” Davidson said the U.S. needs to step up its own information warfare capabilities. “I think we should be putting as much effort into [the information domain] as we’ve been putting into drones and autonomy and things like that in this day and age,” Davidson stated. Chinese hovercraft land on a beach during training. (PLAN) Davidson did not address some other glaring issues in regard to China’s potential seizure of Taiwan. The biggest being will the U.S. actually respond militarily if a major Chinese exercise suddenly became an actual invasion operation? Would there even be enough time and what about China’s anti-access capabilities that could keep much of America’s combat power at bay during the early stages of such a conflict? Would there even be support for such an intervention operation domestically, especially considering it could be very bloody and it would surely manifest itself here at home? Then, as we mentioned in the piece, there are many areas where Taiwan seems to be moving far too slowly while China’s military force continues to balloon on nearly all fronts. Regardless, it’s nice to hear from the man who inadvertently gave birth to the “Davidson Window” now that this ominous window of vulnerability he predicted a half decade is cracking open. Contact the author: howard@twz.com The post ‘Davidson Window’ Admiral Hopes He Was Wrong On China’s Ability To Take Taiwan By 2027 appeared first on TWZ .

title: Watchdog flags fraud, failed Pentagon audit as defense priorities

content:
在五角大楼连续第九次审计失败后几天，其监督办公室将消除欺诈和实现廉洁财务审计列为国防部下一财年最紧迫的战略挑战。随着特朗普政府要求国会提供创纪录的 1.5 万亿美元用于国防，国防部监察长本周发布了一份年度报告，列出了国防部在执行国防战略时面临的七个主要障碍。该办公室表示，优先事项（排名不分先后）包括从威慑中国到振兴国防工业基础，再到支持作战人员和财务透明度。 2026年国防战略将保卫“美国本土”和西半球置于对抗中国之上，并宣布了“特朗普门罗主义的推论”，优先考虑美国在西半球的主导地位以及美国进入巴拿马运河和墨西哥湾的机会。以下是监察长办公室确定的挑战。报告称，“考虑到国防部的广泛业务和庞大的预算，欺诈风险是固有的”，并强调五角大楼拥有最大的可自由支配的联邦预算，并要求国会将其当前资金增加 42%。赫格斯发起反对政府浪费的运动，并承诺消除五角大楼的裁员。
2025 年，在对自己的信号使用情况进行调查时，赫格斯发布了一份备忘录，讨论 IG 办公室的改革问题。他告诉军事领导人，该办公室的系统已经“武器化，让抱怨者、空想家和表现不佳的人坐上驾驶座”。实现干净的财务审计 2018 年，五角大楼首次审计失败后，国会给了国防部 10 年的时间（直到 2028 年 12 月 31 日）通过审计。尽管今年再次失败，但一位官员告诉路透社，审计发现五角大楼 25 个实体中有 14 个通过了财务报表，高于去年的 11 个。审计人员现在正在使用人工智能来处理和测试五角大楼许多过时系统的更多数据。该部门成立了联合审计工作组，该小组由文职人员、军人和私营部门专家组成，旨在解决持续存在的问题。确保有足够的能力保卫美国本土 国防战略将保卫“美国本土”和西半球放在首位。监察长发现部署到美国边境的部队面临压力，并表示目前正在调查国内国民警卫队部署的有效性。该报告还指出了基础设施网络安全和重要设施周围的反无人机能力方面的差距。确保有足够的能力威慑中国 排在第二位的是美国
正在通过在太平洋群岛第一岛链建立强大的态势来重点关注印度-太平洋地区的威慑。监察长发现了“前沿驻扎后勤网络的准备情况、预置设备的条件和可用性、有争议的海上保障路线的弹性以及国防部从美国太平洋司令部责任区多个地点分散和操作空中力量的能力”等问题。  各军种已开始为面向太平洋的战斗做准备。例如，陆军正在加速开发下一代突击倾转旋翼机“Che”

【原文 English Original】
Days after the Pentagon failed its ninth consecutive audit, its oversight office ranked eliminating fraud and achieving a clean financial audit among the Defense Department’s most pressing strategic challenges for the upcoming fiscal year.  As the Trump administration asks Congress for a record $1.5 trillion for national defense, the Department of Defense Inspector General this week released an annual report listing the seven top hurdles facing the department as it executes the National Defense Strategy. The priorities — not ranked in order of priority, according to the office — range from deterring China to energizing the defense-industrial base to supporting warfighters and financial transparency.  The 2026 National Defense Strategy elevated defense of the “U.S. Homeland” and the Western Hemisphere above countering China and declared the “Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine,” prioritizing American dominance in the hemisphere and American access to the Panama Canal and Gulf of Mexico.  Here are the challenges identified by the IG’s office. Eliminating fraud “Considering the Department’s extensive operations and sizeable budget, the risk of fraud is inherent,” the report said, emphasizing that the Pentagon has the largest discretionary federal budget and is asking Congress for a 42% increase in its current funding. Hegseth has campaigned against government waste and pledged to eliminate redundancy in the Pentagon. In 2025, amid an investigation into his own Signal use, Hegseth issued a memo addressing reforms to the IG office. He told military leaders that the office’s systems had been “weaponized, putting complainers, ideologues and poor performers in the driver’s seat.” Achieving a clean financial audit In 2018, after the Pentagon failed its first-ever audit, Congress gave the Defense Department 10 years — until Dec. 31, 2028 — to pass. Though it failed again this year, an official told Reuters that the audit found 14 of 25 Pentagon entities’ passing financial statements, up from 11 the prior year. Auditors are now using artificial intelligence to process and test more data on many of the Pentagon’s outdated systems. The department established Joint Task Force-Audit, which is a group of civilians, service members and private sector experts to address continued issues.  Ensuring sufficient capacity to defend the U.S. homeland The National Defense Strategy places defense of the “U.S. homeland” and Western Hemisphere in the top slot. The IG identified strain on forces deployed to the U.S. border and said it is currently investigating the effectiveness of domestic National Guard deployments. The report also flagged gaps in infrastructure cybersecurity and in counter-unmanned aerial capabilities around important installations.  Ensuring sufficient capacity to deter China Bumped to second priority, the U.S. is focusing on deterrence in the Indo-Pacific by building a strong posture in the First Island Chain, a set of Pacific archipelagos.  The IG identified issues “with the readiness of forward-stationed logistics networks, condition and availability of prepositioned equipment, resilience of contested maritime sustainment routes, and the Department’s ability to disperse and operate airpower from multiple locations in the U.S. Pacific Command area of responsibility.”  The services have begun to prepare for a Pacific-oriented fight. For instance, the Army is accelerating development of its next-generation assault tiltrotor aircraft, the Cheyenne II , designed for use in a Pacific theater.  Increasing burden-sharing with U.S. allies and partners Burden sharing has become a signature phrase for the Trump administration, from discussions about rotational forces in Europe to counterterrorism operations in Africa to deterrence in the Indo-Pacific. The office “identified lessons learned from 10 years of reports related to burden sharing with international partners, noting lack of proper reimbursement by international partners for supplies and services provided by the Department,” the report said. It did not provide specific examples or list the international partners in question. Supercharging the U.S. defense industrial base while ensuring accountability The report said the IG continues to find production shortfalls and, in some cases, a lack of accountability for major defense contractors that fall short of requirements. The Defense Department “is sometimes so dependent on certain contractors that it continues to give them funds even when they fail to deliver or delay delivery by years,” the report said. Additionally, the agency said contractors had not delivered the agreed-upon amount of munitions on time, leading to diminished stockpiles of critical munitions. Earlier this year, the agency also found that the Pentagon’s drive to get weapons faster bypassed acquisition steps meant to ensure new systems work before reaching the force. Supporting the warfighter and their family The new report flagged issues with overseas medical care — including patient safety — the health of trainees, housing quality and issues in the review process for child abuse accusations at childcare centers. According to a new Pentagon directive , all military services must now resolve emergency living conditions within 24 hours or relocate the service member.
